hook: Jamal, 24, slices his palm on a kitchen knife. The bleeding stops in a few minutes, but within the hour the skin around the cut is red, warm, swollen and sore. A week later new skin covers the gap, and a month later a thin pale line is all that remains. Each of those changes has a cause you can trace, starting with the sheet of tissue the knife went through.

prereq.q: A serous membrane lines which kind of space?
options: A tube that opens to the outside of the body
A closed body cavity, such as the pleural cavity
The space inside a single cell
prereq.why: Serous membranes (the pleura, pericardium and peritoneum) line closed body cavities. Their parietal and visceral layers slide on a thin film of serous fluid.

prereq.q: Which connective tissue cell makes collagen fibers?
prereq.why: Fibroblasts make the fibers and ground substance of connective tissue, including collagen. Macrophages engulf debris by phagocytosis, and adipocytes store fat.

prereq.q: What happens to a blood vessel's diameter and the blood flow through it during vasodilation?
prereq.why: In vasodilation the smooth muscle in the vessel wall relaxes, the vessel widens, and resistance falls, so more blood flows through it.

anatomy.caption: The four tissue membranes: mucous membranes line tracts open to the outside, serous membranes line closed body cavities, the cutaneous membrane is your skin, and synovial membranes line the cavities of movable joints.

chain.cause: A cut breaks blood vessels and kills some cells by necrosis.
chain.effect: A blood clot stops the bleeding, and damaged cells and mast cells release histamine and other chemical messengers.

chain.cause: Histamine acts on nearby small arteries, capillaries and the smallest veins.
chain.effect: The small arteries dilate and the small vessels become leaky, so the area turns red, warm and swollen. White blood cells stick to the walls of the smallest veins and crawl out into the tissue.

chain.cause: Macrophages among those white blood cells engulf dead cells and debris by phagocytosis.
chain.effect: The cleared space fills with new capillaries and dividing fibroblasts.

chain.cause: With the gap cleared and supplied with capillaries, surviving working cells beside it divide, if they are a type that can.
chain.effect: Where the framework survived, the new cells regenerate the tissue and its function returns.

chain.cause: Where the working cells cannot divide, or the gap is too large for them to fill, the fibroblasts keep laying down collagen.
chain.effect: The collagen becomes scar tissue (fibrosis), which holds the tissue together but does not do the lost cells' work.

misconception.wrong: Once a wound has healed, the tissue is back to normal.
misconception.right: Healing ends in either regeneration or fibrosis. Only regeneration restores the original working cells. Fibrosis fills the gap with collagen, and scar tissue does not do the lost cells' job: a scar in heart muscle cannot contract, and a scar in the liver does not do liver work. Whether a tissue regenerates depends mainly on whether its working cells can divide and whether its framework survives.

summary: Tissue membranes are sheets that cover or line. Epithelial membranes pair an epithelium with connective tissue: the mucous membrane (mucosa, over a lamina propria) lines tracts open to the outside, the serous membrane lines closed cavities, and the cutaneous membrane is the dry, keratinized skin. The synovial membrane is a connective tissue membrane lining movable joints. Injury starts inflammation: histamine from mast cells dilates small arteries (redness, heat) and makes small vessels leaky (swelling), and chemical messengers cause pain. Macrophages clear the debris; then the tissue regenerates if its working cells (parenchyma) can divide and its framework survives, or fills with collagen as scar tissue (fibrosis) if not. Necrosis is injury-caused cell death that ruptures cells and triggers inflammation; apoptosis does neither.
